title: Model verification playbook — sales & marketing
body:
Purpose:
This playbook gives sales and marketing a concise, usable set of messages, artifacts, and rebuttals for talking about Redwood's model catalog verified profiles for open models. It balances three buyer needs: quality signals, predictable economics, and integration risk reduction.

Context / problem we solve:
- Buyers increasingly choose open models for cost and flexibility but worry about real-world inference performance, hallucination risk, and maintenance overhead.
- Sales needs defensible, measurable claims (not fuzzy adjectives) that can be backed by runtime benchmarks, regressions, and profile metadata.
- Marketing needs repeatable copy/snippets and a simple rubric customers can understand when comparing models.

Core positioning statements (short):
- "Verified profiles: standardized, runtime-backed model facts that make open models predictable for production."
- "We don’t just list models — we measure them across latency, cost-per-token, instruction-following, and hallucination risk under real workloads."
- "Pick a model with a profile that aligns to your SLOs; keep the same API whether hosted, dedicated, or private."

Key reproducible claims (what we can safely say externally):
- CPU/GPU latency percentiles on our standard traces (p50/p95/p99) for 8k/4k/2k contexts.
- Cost per 1k effective tokens on our Dedicated config and hosted pricing bands.
- Instruction-following score on our internal eval harness (dataset and prompt families documented).
- Regression alerting: verified profiles include last-eval-timestamp and delta vs baseline.

Verified profile proposed schema (display-friendly fields):
- model_name (display + canonical id)
- primary_architecture (e.g., LLaMA2-70b)
- verified_at (date)
- metrics: [latency_p50, latency_p95, cost_per_1k_tokens, instruction_score, hallucination_rate_est]
- workload_tags: [chat, code, summarization, retrieval-augmented]
- recommended_deploy: [hosted, dedicated-gpu, quantized-dedicated]
- caveats: short free-text (e.g., "short context bias, struggles with long-form consistency")
- compatible_variants: [int8-quant, 4bit-quant, optimized-kernel]
- sample_prompts: 2–3 representative prompts used for verification

Rubric for internal QA (how a model gets a verified profile):
- Run evaluation harness: latencies under standard trace, instruction score >= X (configurable), hallucination rate below threshold on curated datasets.
- Operational checks: KV cache memory footprint, streaming correctness under 50rps, compat with our fallback routing logic.
- Security/compliance: license check and model weights provenance.
- Results review: assigned reviewer from Applied ML + Product; a short approval note recorded in the profile.

Buyer-facing messaging snippets (ready to paste):
- TL;DR for engineers: "See runtime metrics and example prompts for every model — our verified profiles show p95 latency, cost estimates, and a short list of failure modes so you can pick a model that meets your SLOs."
- For platform execs: "Standardized profiles reduce vendor lock risk by making model behavior comparable and auditable across deployments."
- For procurement/security: "Each profile includes license provenance, last-scanned date, and an audit trail of verification runs."

Competitive snapshot (how to talk vs competitors):
- Vendor A (closed API leader): strengths — turnkey models, predictable behavior; weakness — single provider lock-in, less transparency on per-workload cost. Messaging: "With Redwood you get the flexibility of open models plus runtime-verified facts so you can avoid expensive surprises."
- Vendor B (self-hosted runtime vendor): strengths — low-level control, on-prem options; weakness — integration work and no catalog-level verification. Messaging: "We combine the runtime expertise with a curated catalog and per-model verification to shorten your time-to-confidence."
- Community-run hubs: strengths — breadth; weakness — inconsistent benchmarking and missing operational metadata. Messaging: "Profiles are standardized so you don’t have to re-run dozens of benchmarks to compare models for your workload."

Sales objection handling (short):
- "Open models are risky/stable?" -> "We surface the exact failure modes and provide example prompts with expected output; you can run the same harness in your environment or use our Dedicated preview to validate at scale."
- "How often do profiles change?" -> "Profiles record last-verified date and delta from baseline; major model updates trigger automatic re-verification and a compatibility flag for routing."
- "Is this engineering work?" -> "No — profiles include suggested deploy type and quantization level. For Dedicated or Private customers we can provide a quick proof-of-concept run to reproduce the profile under your infra."

Marketing creative hooks & examples:
- Short headline: "Compare models, not guesswork." Subhead: "Verified runtime facts for open models — latency, cost, and quality where it matters."
- Launch one-pager sections: What a profile contains; How to read the metrics; Use-case examples (chatbot, summarization, code assistant); Quick-start (3 clicks to test).

Measurement plan (what to show in marketing and sales decks):
- Catalog coverage: # models with verified profiles over time (goal: 50+ in 3 months).
- Average time to verification (goal: < 7 days).
- Percent of pilot customers who used a verified profile in selection (goal: 60% of pilots).
- Reduction in trial-to-paid time for Dedicated customers that used profiles vs those that didn’t.

Quick field play (sales enablement assets):
- One-slide cheatsheet: how to read a profile (p50/p95, cost, failure modes).
- 3 short email sequences: intro to profiles, demo invite, trial follow-up with sample prompts.
- Repro script for SEs: link to GitHub runbook that replays the verification harness (include expected flags and where to find sample prompts).

Risks & mitigation (what to avoid saying publicly):
- Don’t claim "perfect" quality or "no hallucinations" — always frame metrics as measured under documented prompts and known failure modes.
- Avoid giving absolute cost numbers for on-prem customers — provide ranges and link to cost-calculator.

Launch checklist (minimal):
- Publish 1-page public explainer + interactive profile viewer on site (marketing).
- Enable filter in Catalog UI by workload_tags and latency buckets (product).
- Create SE runbook + demo tenant with 5 verified models (solutions).
- PR/announce: blog post with methodology & dataset links; webinar with Applied ML lead.

Open questions (items for next iterations):
- Standardize hallucination metric (need consensus across applied-ml and product).
- Decide default thresholds for instruction_score that map to "recommended" vs "experimental" badges.
- Explore embedding similarity to detect drift in model outputs over time as an automated re-verification signal.

Appendix: example short profile (for copy):
- Name: rwd-llama2-13b-v1
- Verified: 2026-01-18
- p50/p95 latency (4k seq, Dedicated T4): 45ms / 180ms
- cost per 1k effective tokens: $0.12 (hosted estimate)
- instruction_score: 87 (higher is better)
- hallucination_rate_est: 4.7% (on curated KB tasks)
- tags: chat, summarization
- sample prompt: "Summarize this support thread in 3 bullets and highlight customer intent."

Next steps (who does what):
- Applied ML: finalize hallucination metric proposal (owner: Ravi) — due 2026-03-15.
- Product: finalize UI layout for public profile page (owner: Sophie) — due 2026-03-01.
- Marketing: draft public explainer & blog (owner: Marina) — first draft due 2026-02-20 (in progress).

Notes: link to slack thread #catalog-verifications, see confluence CATALOG-VERIF-OVERVIEW-4821 for methodology detail.

Draft status: this is a go-to-market draft intended for internal alignment. Please comment directly in the doc with objections or missing use-cases.
